title: Diving Deeper into Caroline Ong's Math is Beautiful High Horse, In Her Own Words -words
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This piece features an extended, largely first-person account from Texas math teacher Caroline Ong, explaining the mechanics behind her "math is beautiful high horse," brief, tangential mini-sermons about the value and beauty of mathematics that she delivers to students. Ong describes her "free lecture" concept: alongside the paid-for math instruction, she offers a philosophical lecture on the importance of math or effective studying, delivered from a physically different spot in the room to signal the shift in mode. Stuart highlights three things he notices in her account: the intentionality of using consistent physical space to mark different types of instruction, her generosity in sharing an unpolished glimpse of her practice, and her free-lecture habit of explicitly teaching students things, like how to study, that are often wrongly assumed to be already known. The piece functions as a practitioner case study that gives concrete texture to Stuart's more abstract "Apologist Winsome and Sure" concept.
points: Ong's "free lecture" concept distinguishes paid-for content instruction from an explicit, separate philosophical case for why the discipline matters and how to study it.
She uses a consistent physical location shift, stepping to the side, as a nonverbal signal that she's moving from instruction into value-building commentary.
Stuart highlights that Ong doesn't assume students already know how to study or learn effectively, she teaches those meta-skills directly, addressing a common but under-examined gap.
The piece models how one teacher's unscripted, personality-driven practice can be shared as a generalizable case study for colleagues.
quotes: I am a great fan of using analogies to illustrate and teach — my 'high horse' is when I want to pontificate about some sort of bigger idea not directly related to the mathematical lesson of the day.

Sometimes, I also refer to this as the 'free lecture.' There's the lecture you pay for — the math lecture — and then there's the philosophical lecture about the importance of mathematics, or how to be a good student.

I'll generally just step aside from my usual lecture spot — just a different spot from where I typically deliver instruction. Being a creature of habit, my pontificating generally happens in the same spot, too, over to the side.
That intentionality of doing the same things from the same spots is sharp. She gives direct instruction from one spot; she does her "math is beautiful high horse" work from another.
She doesn't assume they know how to study; she teaches them how. She doesn't assume they know how to learn effectively; she teaches them how. This is so important for so many of the five key beliefs.
